newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries end down, profit-taking, Fed, supply.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries end down, profit-taking, Fed, supply.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries closed slightly lower on Wednesday as players took some profits while digesting new remarks by several top Federal Reserve officials and a fresh government debt auction.
The 6.625-percent 30-year benchmark Treasury bond ended down 6/32 at 102-18/32. Its yield was at 6.43 percent.

Although prices fell modestly, analysts said the market's overall performance was positive, given the strong rally seen on Tuesday, when the bellwether skyrocketed more than one-and- a-half points at the close.
"The market traded very well in the wake of yesterday's gigantic rally. We had no problem remaining around new highs," said Patrick Dimick, bond strategist at UBS Securtities.

Prices see-sawed mildly as traders spent most of the day in front of their screens, scrutinizing news headlines from Washington, where Fed chairman Alan Greenspan delivered the second leg of his Humphrey-Hawkins testimony on Wednesday.

Also in the nation's capital, Fed vice-chair Alice Rivlin shared the stage with Fed governor Laurence Meyer and New York Fed president William McDonough for a previously-scheduled hearing at the House Banking Committee.

Greenspan told senators Wednesday that he thought it was possible to reduce the inflation premium in long-term rates further. The chairman's remarks came during the question-and- answer session. His speech to the Senate Wednesday was similar to the one he delivered to the House a day before.
"The market grabbed a quick quarter-point bid on those comments," said a senior trader at a U.S. investment bank.

Analysts said, however, Greenspan's remarks were offset by some hawkish comments by Rivlin and Meyer. The fed vice-chair said, among other things, that she believed the risk of more inflation outweighs downside recession risks.
Meyer said the Fed must not wait until inflation takes off, adding that the central bank needs to be preemptive.

"The comments by Fed officials today were just a little bit less warm and fuzzy than were the comments yesterday by Fed chairman Greenspan," said Ward McCarthy, managing director at consulting firm Stone and McCarthy Research Associates.

"But the differences of opinion, clearly, are fairly limited and I think the overall implication is still pretty good from the market's perspective ... Fed policy is on hold here possibly for a prolonged period of time," he added.
Analysts said the underlying trend in the market remains bullish, but they warned that the upside potential for the short-end of the yield curve is limited.
They said the spread between the two-year note and the federal funds rate has narrowed to 36 basis points from 40 basis points earlier in the week.
Pundits said that gap was unlikely to get any narrower unless the market started to price in an easing of monetary policy. But that possibility was discounted by most analysts.
"I don't think there is any reason to be terribly pessimistic on the market.

"But at current yield levels and (in) the absence of some deterioration in economic activity that would raise the specter of a Fed easing, you have to wonder to what extent the upside potential for the market is limited," McCarthy said.
Traders said the market was perceived to be slightly overbought. But they added Treasuries could rally a little further before some strong profit-taking took place.
"We have seen the spread between the two-year and fed funds at 32 basis points in the past, and we could see it again," said a trader at a primary dealership.
Also on Wednesday, players snapped up the Treasury's sale of $11.5 billion in five-year notes.
The issues were well-bid and ended up being placed at 6.024 percent, well below expectations. The bid-to-cover ratio was 2.88, with 87 percent of the bids awarded at high.
The three-month Treasury bill rate closed down two basis points at 5.06 percent. The six-month bill rate fell one point to 5.13 percent. The year bill rate was up one point at 5.23 percent.

The two-year note closed down 1/32 at 100-1/32, yielding 5.86 percent. The five-year note traded off 2/32 at 100-25/32 to yield 6.06 percent. The ten-year note closed down 5/32 at 103-15/32, yielding 6.15 percent.
